slides.title: More than a dozen churches claimed to own Jesus's foreskin.
A theology problem
slides.body: Doctrine holds that Christ rose and ascended bodily, leaving little behind. But Luke's Gospel says he was circumcised on the eighth day.

slides.title: Even the pope wouldn't pick
slides.body: The abbey of Charroux claimed one; so did the papal chapel at the Lateran in Rome. In the early 1200s Pope Innocent III declined to rule on which was real.

slides.title: Looted in the Sack of Rome
slides.body: Local tradition says a German soldier took the Lateran relic in 1527 and hid it near Calcata, north of Rome. The village paraded it every 1 January.

slides.title: Don't even talk about it
slides.body: According to the journalist David Farley, a Vatican decree of 1900 threatened excommunication for anyone who wrote or spoke about the relic.

slides.title: Then it vanished
slides.body: In 1983 Calcata's priest announced it had been stolen from his home. Thieves after its jeweled case, or a quiet church removal? It has never resurfaced.

caption: Medieval Europe had too many holy foreskins, and the most famous one vanished from a priest's home in 1983. Who do you think took it?
xPost: More than a dozen medieval churches claimed to own Jesus's foreskin, sometimes at the same time. A pope declined to say which was real. One ended up in the Italian village of Calcata. In 1983 it was reported stolen, and it has never resurfaced.
